video_title: A.I. To Cause Even Higher Inflation & Interest Rates? | Jim Bianco
gist: Jim Bianco argues the bigger AI risk is that it works: a boom in real growth would push nominal growth and thus Treasury, mortgage and corporate rates sharply higher and break low-return business models, with agentic AI already threatening bank deposit franchises and subscription models. With ~3% sticky inflation and ~2.5% real growth, he sees 5-6% yields as normal, has turned buyer of bonds for the first time in six years, and frames a '4-5-6' return world in which the S&P is split into an AI market and a ~6%-returning non-AI market.

themes.theme: AI success risk: growth, inflation, higher rates

insights.claim: Jim Bianco argues the bigger AI risk is not a bubble bursting and AI companies defaulting, but the technology actually delivering on much of its promise, which would bring much faster growth, much higher inflation and much higher interest rates.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Positioning only for an AI bust leaves portfolios exposed to the opposite scenario: a structurally higher-rate, higher-growth regime.
insights.quote: I think it's more along the lines of what if the technology does actually deliver on some or most of its promise.

insights.claim: Bianco believes all technologies end in a bubble, including AI, but the AI bubble is still expanding and its eventual peak may be years away.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Argues against shorting or exiting AI exposure too early on bubble grounds alone.
insights.quote: this bubble is expanding and it might be years before we eventually see that peak in the bubble

insights.claim: Bianco's framework: the long-term interest rate should sit roughly at nominal GDP growth, so an AI-boosted economy growing 4-5% real with ~3% inflation implies 7-8% Treasury yields, ~9-10% mortgage rates and 8-9% corporate borrowing costs.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: If AI lifts real growth sustainably, long-duration bonds and rate-sensitive assets reprice sharply lower.
insights.quote: I've argued that the long-term interest rate for an economy should be about where your nominal growth is.

insights.claim: Bianco says the president has suggested US GDP could grow 20% if AI fulfills its promise; the US economy has never grown 20%, and Bianco now puts sustained boom-level growth odds at small but above zero, versus essentially zero 18-24 months ago.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Tail scenario of explosive growth is now non-zero and should be considered in rate and equity scenarios.
insights.quote: today I would say the odds are now off zero but very small but they're off zero

insights.claim: An AI-driven high-growth economy would force businesses growing only 2-4% (corner grocery stores, new restaurants, LPs) to show 8-10% returns or restructure, because the opportunity cost of money rises for everyone.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Low-growth, financing-dependent business models are the losers in an AI-success world; transition is painful even if ultimately positive.

insights.claim: Bianco calls the cost of money (interest rates) the most important statistic in finance, because every investment decision starts with the opportunity cost of capital.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Anchors all asset valuation to the rate regime; a rising opportunity cost reprices everything.
insights.quote: The most important statistic in all of financial finance is the cost of money is interest rates.

insights.claim: A two-tiered rate system in which slow-growing firms get cheap 3% loans while fast-growing firms pay 8-9% would invert the risk scale and subvert the incentive role of the cost of money, so Bianco rejects it as a solution.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Expect policy arguments for selective cheap credit to be distortionary; cheap money would just be arbitraged into higher-return uses (malinvestment).

insights.claim: Bianco models the AI path on the internet: after the NASDAQ's 83% bubble crash in 2000-2002 the internet still delivered, and the index rose nearly 20x over the following 20 years.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Even a bubble pop would not invalidate the long-term AI thesis; the post-crash winners compounded massively.

themes.theme: AI labor displacement and social backlash

insights.claim: Adam Taggart worries that AI and robotics could displace tens of millions of lower-skill US workers faster than the economy can reabsorb them, and combined with a higher cost of money this creates a double whammy for households, citing Keynes' warning on the pace of technological displacement.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart (host)
insights.so_what: Fast displacement raises social and political risk that could prompt policy backlash against AI beneficiaries.

insights.claim: Bianco notes the most common low-skilled job in the US is driver (taxi, truck, forklift, bus), and AI efforts are aimed at automating all of them, which he expects to strain social cohesion.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Autonomous driving is the largest single labor-displacement vector; watch for regulatory/political pushback.
insights.quote: the most common lowskilled job in the United States is driver and we're going right at

insights.claim: Bianco draws on the 19th-century railroad boom (and the book '1873' on that year's crash): the railroad-driven industrial revolution took 40-50 years and its disruption produced backlash like Marx's Communist Manifesto, whereas AI is attempting similar change in years or a decade.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Compressed timeline raises the odds of sharper political backlash than past technology transitions.
insights.quote: We're talking about doing this in years or a decade.

insights.claim: George Pullman, whom Bianco calls the Sam Altman or Dario Amodei of the railroad era, was buried in Chicago with his crypt encased in feet of cement out of fear the public would dig him up over railroad disruption; Bianco stresses the backlash came because the technology worked, not because it failed.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Public animosity toward AI leaders is a plausible second-order risk if AI succeeds.
insights.quote: it was a transition because it worked. It wasn't a transition because it failed

themes.theme: Agentic AI vs. friction-based business models

insights.claim: Bianco says Meta's personal AI agent Muse, launched about six weeks ago, became the number one downloaded app within days thanks to Meta's ~2 billion Facebook users.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Distribution scale lets Meta rapidly put agents in consumers' hands, accelerating disruption of incumbent business models.

insights.claim: Over the six weeks since Muse launched, bank stocks fell every week for six consecutive weeks for the first time since 2008, with the KBW bank index down about 15%.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Bank weakness may reflect deposit-franchise disruption from AI agents rather than a credit problem.

insights.claim: Bianco highlights roughly $4 trillion sitting in zero-interest bank checking accounts, earning banks well over $120 billion a year, which AI agents can erode by auto-sweeping idle balances into money market funds daily.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Bank net interest margins on cheap deposits are at risk; money market fund managers could gain flows.
insights.quote: There's $4 trillion that sits in bank accounts with zero interest payments

insights.claim: Bianco reports that banks downplayed agentic sweeping as trivial but on Friday announced a ban on AI agents moving money between accounts, which he frames as the possible beginning of an 'agentic AI bank run'.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Bank defensiveness signals they see the deposit threat; watch for regulatory fights and deposit-beta changes.
insights.quote: we might be seeing the beginning of an angentic AI bank run

insights.claim: No bank has yet reported losing deposits to agentic sweeps, so Bianco reads the ban as banks anticipating a potential tidal wave once the behavior becomes widely accepted.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: The deposit-flight risk is prospective; monitor bank deposit data for early evidence.

insights.claim: Bianco says Planet Fitness and The New York Times stocks are suffering because AI agents can check usage and cancel unused subscriptions instantly, removing the consumer laziness their models depend on; he expects streaming services to face the same pressure.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Subscription businesses reliant on inertia/churn friction face structural pressure; screen for 'laziness-dependent' revenue.
insights.quote: a lot of business models in 2026 are based on the idea that we're lazy

insights.claim: Bianco notes zero-interest deposits let banks subsidize small accounts with low or no fees, so if agents compress bank margins, small-balance customers could lose those subsidies.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Second-order effect: bank fee structures may rise, partly offsetting consumer gains from agents.

insights.claim: Taggart suggests agent-driven savings may widen the wealth gap, since sweeping idle cash matters far more to people with significant assets than to someone with a small checking balance.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart (host)
insights.so_what: AI consumer benefits may accrue disproportionately to asset holders.

themes.theme: Normal rates: bonds back at fair value

insights.claim: Bianco argues the 2010-2020 era of zero and negative rates was the most abnormal period in 5,000 years of interest-rate history (per Homer and Sylla's 'A History of Interest Rates'), and today's ~5% rates are normal, not too high.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Investors anchored to ZIRP will misjudge 5% as restrictive; don't expect a return to near-zero rates.
insights.quote: That was the most abnormal thing that we have ever seen arguably in the history of finance.

insights.claim: Bianco expects roughly 3% inflation and about 2.5% real growth, implying 5-6% nominal growth and therefore 5-6% as the appropriate level for interest rates.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Gives a fair-value anchor: yields below 5% look expensive, near 7% would look too punitive.

insights.claim: At the start of October, for the first time in six years, Bianco said he likes and is buying bonds, because Treasury yields from the 3-year to the 30-year were all between 5% and 6%, no longer expensive though not cheap.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Bianco is a buyer of Treasuries across the curve at 5-6% yields.
insights.quote: for the first time in six years, I said, I like bonds. I'm going to buy bonds.

insights.claim: Bianco sees little risk of yields rising to 6-8% and expects bond prices to roughly hold, letting investors capture the ~5% yield, unlike at 4% yields where rising yields would produce near-zero total return, as happened this year.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Favorable asymmetry for carry-focused bond buyers now versus earlier in the year.
insights.quote: I can grab a fiveish% yield and have little risk of loss

insights.claim: Bianco does not expect a multi-year bond rally, because that would require growth to severely disappoint or inflation to fall sharply, and he sees neither for now; a settlement of both wars lowering oil would only help at the margin.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Buy bonds for income, not big capital gains.

insights.claim: Bianco argues rates that are too low are also harmful because they fund speculative excess and malinvestment and create inflation; cheap money for a 3%-growth business would just be levered into 20% opportunities.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Push for financial repression would raise inflation and speculation risk.

insights.claim: Taggart reports that Jan van Eck, at the Thoughtful Money conference, attributed rising bond yields primarily to economic growth rather than inflation fears, war or oil, a view corroborated by other presenters.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart (host)
insights.so_what: Supports reading higher yields as a growth signal rather than a stress signal.

insights.claim: Bianco says the US is running about a 6% deficit-to-GDP in non-crisis good times, among the highest peacetime levels in history, comparable only to COVID, the GFC, the World Wars and the Civil War.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Persistent large deficits keep inflation and term premium elevated, supporting higher yields.

insights.claim: Federal government spending is about 23% of GDP, a level Bianco says has only been exceeded in existential crises like COVID, World War II or the Civil War, and he calls peacetime spending the biggest problem the US faces.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Fiscal dominance risk keeps upward pressure on rates.

insights.claim: Bianco argues high debt is a reason rates should stay higher, not lower, and that forcing rates down via financial repression (as the president and Treasury Secretary want) to subsidize spending would only create more inflation and hurt the bottom of the K-shaped economy.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Political pressure for lower rates is an inflation risk; watch Fed independence.

insights.claim: Bianco notes neither party shows interest in curbing spending, citing a proposed $5,000 payment to voters ahead of the midterms, which he calls a bribe.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: More fiscal stimulus adds to inflation and deficit pressure.

insights.claim: Bianco argues low US inflation from 2001-2020 was imported: after China joined the WTO, core goods PCE (about a third of core) averaged about -0.5% while services inflation averaged about 2.5%, so policymakers mistook a China trade effect for inflation control.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Without goods deflation, 2% inflation is unattainable; expect ~3% sticky inflation.

insights.claim: Because both parties learned globalization's costs (e.g., 'Deaths of Despair' by Case and Deaton), Bianco expects no return to goods deflation, leaving the US stuck at roughly 3% inflation.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Structural inflation floor around 3% argues against expecting deep rate cuts.
insights.quote: we're not going to go back to goods deflation. So, we're stuck at threeish percent inflation.

insights.claim: Bianco cites BYD's Seal 6 (a Tesla Model 3 lookalike) at about $15,000 and the Seagull at about $10,000 as examples of cheap Chinese EVs banned in the US and now restricted in Europe to protect domestic auto industries.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Illustrates the deflation-versus-domestic-industry trade-off; protectionism keeps goods prices elevated.

insights.claim: Bianco says the Redfin price per square foot is at or within half a percent of its all-time high, so housing is fine at current mortgage rates and these are appropriate rate levels.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Housing is not breaking under 7-8% mortgages; affordability rather than price is the stress.

insights.claim: Bianco argues cutting mortgage rates by 200bp would just raise home prices, since the average US home (~$420,000) costs about $3,400 a month all-in and sellers would price to keep that payment; the real fix for affordability is more supply, blocked by homeowner NIMBY zoning.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Rate cuts are not a housing affordability solution; supply-side policy matters more.

insights.claim: Bianco frames housing as a 40/60 tension: about 40% of Americans rent and want lower prices, while about 60% own and want higher prices, and the last attempt to bridge it with exotic mortgages nearly blew up the financial system.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Expect political resistance to policies that lower home prices.

insights.claim: Taggart counters that a 200bp mortgage rate cut could unlock locked-in sellers and flood inventory; Bianco responds that 30-40% of low-rate mortgage holders have already transacted, with over half expected within a couple of years.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart (host)
insights.so_what: The mortgage lock-in effect is gradually fading, increasing supply over time.

themes.theme: Return expectations and two stock markets

insights.claim: Bianco frames the current environment as a '4-5-6 world': about 4% cash, 5% bonds and roughly 6% (maybe 7%) stocks, and warns investors not to feel entitled to 20-30% annual returns.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Recalibrate return expectations; bonds at 5% look attractive relative to equities' expected ~6%.

insights.claim: Bianco says a list of about 41 AI-related stocks (sourced from JPMorgan) made up about 49% of S&P 500 market cap last week, the highest thematic concentration since 19th-century railroads.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Index exposure is effectively a concentrated AI bet; diversification is less than it appears.

insights.claim: Bianco says the S&P ex-AI and S&P AI baskets have turned negatively correlated, creating effectively two stock markets: the ~459 non-AI stocks are up about 6-6.5% this year while the S&P's ~15% gain is driven by AI names, especially semis.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Read index moves carefully; non-AI equities are delivering returns consistent with a ~6% world.
insights.quote: there's effectively two stock markets right now

insights.claim: Last week the S&P 500 fell while the non-AI stocks rose; Bianco attributes the decline to a handful of neoclouds scaring investors rather than economic weakness.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Don't infer macro weakness from index declines driven by AI names.

insights.claim: Bianco argues that if AI works, the 459 non-AI companies will be forced to change rather than ride along, so owning the whole index is not a safe diversification hedge.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Non-AI incumbents face disruption risk in the AI-success scenario.

insights.claim: Bianco downplays CoreWeave (about $30 billion of debt) as a credit canary, noting Tricolor and First Brands failures a year ago did not derail private credit, which wobbled but survived.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: An AI-credit default would likely be idiosyncratic rather than systemic.
